solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Why northerner can't smoke in retirement club?

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the reason is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: a northerner's excuse: 'no tab', tab being northern English slang for a cigarette

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about why a man from the north of England may not light up at his retirement club.
explanation.walkthrough: NO TAB written backwards gives BATON. 'Club' looks like a social club in the surface, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton is a police truncheon, a short stick used as a weapon, i.e. a club.

clue.text: When dons scold son for interest levels

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing, so the other piece is worn around this one

blocks.note: to berate is to scold
as in 'as the sun rose'
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: University teachers telling a student off about the cost of borrowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university tutors; it is the verb meaning puts on, so the scolding word is worn around the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Base rates are the benchmark interest rates set by a central bank, so they are levels of interest.

clue.text: In what manner grips run after tense cast

indicators.note: gripping something means holding it tight inside
after means placed following the other piece

blocks.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
how asks in what way
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Asking how an anxious angler grips the line before casting.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw something is to cast it, as in casting a stone.

clue.text: Those against boxing in explosive runners

indicators.note: boxing something means enclosing it in a box, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: those voting against are the noes
a mine is an explosive device

explanation.surface: Opponents of boxing among athletes, as if boxers were dangerous racers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runners' looks like athletes or horses, but it means candidates running for a post.
explanation.definitionFit: Nominees are candidates put forward for an election or award, people who are running.

clue.text: Initial advantage of saint visiting madam?

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's place, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a brothel madam is, jokingly, the chief prostitute: head tart
S is an abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A holy figure calling on a lady of the house, oddly described as an initial advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the cheeky view of a brothel madam as the top prostitute. Saint here is the single-letter abbreviation, not the usual two.
explanation.definitionFit: A head start is a lead given or gained at the beginning of a race or contest.

clue.text: Level of spice in Goethe: a truckload

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the poet's name and the following words

explanation.surface: Literary criticism: Goethe's work is packed with spice by the truckload.
explanation.definitionFit: The heat of a chilli dish is how hot or spicy it is.

clue.text: Men eat more after playing a wind instrument

indicators.note: playing about with something rearranges it freely

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A jibe that blokes eat more after playing a trumpet or tuba.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind instrument' suggests a trumpet, and the joke about flatulence after eating; here it is a device that measures wind.
explanation.definitionFit: An anemometer is a meteorological instrument that measures wind speed, so literally a wind instrument.

clue.text: Grey-haired flake promoting India

indicators.note: promoting moves something up a rank, and in a down answer up means earlier in the word

blocks.note: a sliver is a thin flake or splinter
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An elderly eccentric pushing the cause of India.
explanation.walkthrough: The I in SLIVER moves up one place. 'Flake' looks like slang for an unreliable person; it is a thin piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Silver hair is grey or white, so silver describes someone grey-haired.

clue.text: Fresh Madeira cakes Illinois sent via Dakota?

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement
cakes as a verb means coats or covers, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: the fodder letters
IL is the US postal abbreviation for Illinois

explanation.surface: Fresh Madeira cakes shipped from Illinois to the Dakotas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dakota' looks like the US state, which fits Illinois; it is the Douglas DC-3 Dakota aircraft. 'Cakes' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Something airmailed is sent by aeroplane, and the Dakota was a classic transport plane, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Having lost heart, con hoovers up a line

indicators.note: losing the heart means the middle letter is removed
hoovering up something sucks it inside

blocks.note: a con is a trick
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dispirited convict vacuuming up a line of cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: TRICK loses its middle I, and A fills the gap. Hoover is British for a vacuum cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: A track is a line or path, such as a railway line.

clue.text: Fight small publication involved in offence

indicators.note: something involved in a matter is caught up inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
an offence against the law
short for magazine

explanation.surface: A minor magazine being dragged into a criminal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fight' could be wordplay for a bout, but it is the definition; the small publication is a magazine shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrimmage is a confused struggle or scuffle, a rough fight.

clue.text: Rock on the radio for a nit?

indicators.note: radio is heard not seen, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: lava is molten rock that hardens into rock; in a non-rhotic British accent the two words sound the same

explanation.surface: Asking what song a radio station plays for a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nit' looks like the British word for an idiot, which the surface of a rock-music radio show suits; here it is the young louse. Lava and larva sound alike in British speech, where the R is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A nit is the egg or young form of a louse, so loosely an immature insect, a larva; the question mark admits the stretch.

clue.text: Individual contracted to separate band in dispute

indicators.note: a contracted word has been shortened, here losing its final letter
something that separates a thing pushes into its middle and splits it in two

blocks.note: a ring is a circular band
one's own, individual to oneself

explanation.surface: A solo contractor called in to break up a feuding pop group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like a group of musicians, but it is a ring; 'individual' is the adjective as in one's own.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are rowing are quarrelling noisily, so they are in dispute with each other.

clue.text: Return no-good rubbish delivered by Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words trade their first sounds

blocks.note: bum as an adjective means worthless or poor quality
cack is British slang for rubbish or excrement
the opening sounds of the two words swap places

explanation.surface: Dismissing a worthless retort as rubbish uttered by the famously muddled Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping B and C: bum cack becomes cum back, pronounced come back.
explanation.definitionFit: A comeback is a return, either to former success or as a quick reply.

clue.text: Awfully game red and dominant lady in a field

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A hunting scene: plenty of red game and a lady lording it over the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Field' suggests a hunt or meadow; it means a sphere of activity.
explanation.definitionFit: A grande dame is an elderly, respected woman who dominates her profession or area of work.

clue.text: Labour energy taxes: soft soap and flannel?

blocks.note: to labour is to toil
E is the symbol for energy in physics
something that taxes your patience tries it

explanation.surface: A political jibe: Labour's energy taxes are nothing but flattery and evasive talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour with a capital looks like the British political party; it is just work. Soft soap and flannel both also mean smooth talk, which the surface uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Soap and a face cloth (a flannel in Britain) are examples of toiletries, articles used for washing, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Something that drew loads of people out West?

definitions.text: Something that drew loads of people out West?

blocks.clueFragment: Something that drew loads of people out West?
blocks.note: surface reading: an attraction that pulled crowds to the American frontier
setter's reading: drew means pulled, like a horse, carrying loads of passengers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drew' reads as attracted, but it is hauled, as a horse draws a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron horse was the Native American and Wild West nickname for the steam locomotive that hauled trains across the frontier.

clue.text: Half-cut tramp opening for Pete and Dud

indicators.note: cutting a word by half leaves only its first half
the opening of a word is its very first letter

blocks.note: a tramp in the sense of a promiscuous woman is a floozy
first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A drunk vagrant at the start of a Peter Cook and Dudley Moore show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' (British for tipsy) and 'Pete and Dud' (Cook and Moore's comedy double act) suggest a comic sketch; Dud is the definition. FLOOZY halved leaves FLO.
explanation.definitionFit: A dud is something that fails completely, and a flop is likewise a failure.

clue.text: By a loch, an old maid endlessly drinking Old Pride

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
drinking takes something inside, so one piece holds the other
by means beside, so the pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: the stereotypical old maid is prim and prudish
O is the abbreviation for old
Loch Ness in Scotland

explanation.surface: A spinster beside a Scottish lake, drinking an old-style ale called Old Pride.
explanation.walkthrough: PRUDE loses its last letter, then holds O. 'Old Pride' looks like a beer's name; the second Old is only O.
explanation.definitionFit: Proudness is the state of being proud, which is the same as pride.

clue.text: An insatiable female great-white shark

blocks.note: first meaning: a woman who devours one lover after another
second meaning: a fish known for attacking people

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one predatory woman described as a shark; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a woman with many lovers whom she discards and an animal, such as a great white, that attacks humans.

clue.text: Steaming after the last of this?

definitions.text: Steaming after the last of this?

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter only

blocks.note: final letter of the word
something steaming is very hot

explanation.surface: Wondering whether one is drunk after finishing off one more drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts HOT behind the S. Steaming is British slang for very drunk, and as a whole the clue describes a glass of spirits that leaves you that way.
explanation.definitionFit: A shot is a small measure of spirits, the sort of drink after which one may end up steaming drunk.

clue.text: One with dog and errant bats as concerns

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the letters before it go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: Roman numeral for one
the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Someone with a dog and some stray bats, all strangely relating to some matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errant' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'bats' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: In regard to is a formal phrase meaning concerning, as concerns or with reference to.

clue.text: One avoiding more theatrical clobber

indicators.note: avoiding something means leaving it out, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: Roman numeral for one
a ham actor overacts, so a hammier one is more theatrical

explanation.surface: An actor who steers clear of the more melodramatic costumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like British slang for clothes, which fits the theatre; it is the verb to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: To clobber someone is to hit them hard, and to hammer them means the same.

clue.text: A French nut taking in the French Open?

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: un is French for a
nut is slang for the head
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A French lunatic playing at the French Open tennis tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French Open' reads as the tennis Grand Slam; Open alone is the definition, with the French article tucked inside the nut.
explanation.definitionFit: An unhealed wound is still open, not yet closed over; the question mark marks the definition by example.

clue.text: Put out unopened box of matching mugs

indicators.note: not opened means the first letter is missing

blocks.note: a box of mugs that match is a cup set

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed at receiving a sealed gift box of matching mugs.
explanation.walkthrough: CUP SET loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To be put out is to be annoyed or offended, which is to be upset.

clue.text: Note that's on about my past performance

indicators.note: in an across clue, a piece that is on another comes after it

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like my!
D is a note of the musical scale

explanation.surface: A memo concerning one's own history of achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive, but it is an exclamation, as in 'My, how you've grown!'
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's record, such as a track record, is the account of their achievements so far.

clue.text: Love sex, but not with you and a veggie

indicators.note: not with you means the letter standing for you, as in text speak, is taken away

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
sexual union

explanation.surface: A rejection: happy to have love and sex, just not with you and a vegetarian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veggie' suggests a vegetarian person; it is a vegetable. U is text-speak for you.
explanation.definitionFit: An onion is a vegetable, and veggie is informal for vegetable.

clue.text: Leg it and consume apace in bar

blocks.note: first meaning: run away
second meaning: eat food quickly
third meaning: a sliding bar that fastens a door

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone dashing into a pub and gulping a drink; there are three separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to flee suddenly, to gobble food, and a metal rod used to secure a door.

clue.text: Antidote for non-union employment: liquor

indicators.note: non- means without, and the abbreviation for union is taken away

blocks.note: use is employment, as in putting something to use
rum is an alcoholic spirit

explanation.surface: Drink offered as the cure for working without a union.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the usual abbreviation for union, so USE without U leaves SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A serum, specifically an antiserum, carries antibodies that counteract venom or disease, serving as an antidote.

clue.text: Fit into a schedule at last!

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it

blocks.note: a time, as in a scheduled time
a fit or bout of coughing

explanation.surface: Relief at finally squeezing something into a busy diary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit into' reads as one verb; Fit is the noun BOUT, and it goes into A TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: About time! is an exclamation of impatience when something finally happens, much like at last!

clue.text: Their tone upset East Asia

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters fall into a different order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Their manner of speaking offends the people of East Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orient is an old-fashioned name for the countries of the East, especially East Asia.

clue.text: Doctors covering the first of 999 calls

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it, so one piece goes outside the other
the first of something here means only its opening letter

blocks.note: to doctor results is to rig them
999 is said nine nine nine, beginning with N

explanation.surface: Medics answering emergency calls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' looks like medics; it is the verb meaning falsifies. 999 is the British emergency phone number.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring someone is to phone them, so rings means calls.
